overview: Natal was a British colony on southern Africa’s Indian Ocean coast, with African communities, settler farms and towns, and Indian workers and traders. Plantation labour, schools and printing presses all shaped its history. It was distinct from the neighboring Zulu kingdom.

periods.title: Annexation and administration
periods.summary: Britain annexed Natal in 1843; a separate colonial charter followed in 1856.

periods.title: Colony and migration
periods.summary: Indian indentured migration began in 1860. Natal joined the Union of South Africa in 1910.

items.text: The colony’s dates begin before this map record. Britain annexed Natal in 1843 and initially administered it from the Cape; Natal became a separate colony in 1856. The imported 1878 starting point is a surviving map snapshot, not the founding year.

Natal was a British colony while the Zulu kingdom remained a separate African state. Britain’s 1878 ultimatum demanded changes that would destroy Zulu independence, and invasion followed in 1879. Their proximity on a map must not erase the distinction between colony and kingdom.

The Truro arrived in November 1860 with Indian indentured workers. Their contracts supplied labour to colonial employers, especially plantations. Later Indian traders also came independently, so “Indian migrant” did not describe one occupation or one route into Natal.

Historian Jo Beall documents women plucking tender tea leaves on Natal estates. Men and children also worked in estate production, with tasks divided by age and gender. Tea in a cup concealed a demanding sequence of picking, carrying and processing.

Women’s work continued after paid estate tasks. Household duties and small garden plots helped feed children and adults. Beall’s research places this less visible labour beside employers’ records, showing why a wage or contract alone cannot describe a family’s working day.

In 1861 Bauboo Naidoo opened a shop in Durban’s Field Street selling condiments and foods missing from workers’ rations. The tiny detail matters: migration carried tastes and cooking knowledge, and people sought familiar ingredients rather than simply accepting an employer’s menu.

John and Nokutela Dube founded Ohlange in 1901 after gaining experience in the United States. The school connected education with African institution-building. Remembering both founders keeps Nokutela’s contribution visible beside the much more frequently named John Dube.

A short isiZulu writing sample is “Ilanga lase Natal”, meaning “The Natal Sun”. The newspaper began under John Dube at Ohlange in 1903. A newspaper title could announce a public voice in a reader’s own language before they had read a single article.

The surviving Ilanga collection allows readers to study an African newspaper as a sequence of issues, rather than only a famous editor’s biography. Its establishment at Ohlange links a school to the work of printing and distributing information.

At Phoenix, a printing press became part of a communal settlement. Gandhi bought the land in 1904 and moved the press for Indian Opinion there from Durban. Producing a newspaper involved physical work as well as ideas: the entire press had to change address.

Phoenix residents cultivated food gardens and experimented with communal self-sufficiency. The settlement also provided meals, accommodation and education for families of people involved in nonviolent protest campaigns. Political activity depended on ordinary tasks such as feeding children and keeping a place to sleep.

Recruitment of Indian indentured labour for Natal ended in 1911 after decades of mistreatment and controversy. The workers and their descendants did not disappear when recruitment stopped; Indian South African communities continued building families, businesses, associations and public lives.

ending.text: Natal joined the Union of South Africa on 31 May 1910 and became a province. Its communities continued through this change of government. The map record extends to 1914, but that endpoint is not the colony’s constitutional ending.
